title: Broad-spectrum treatment for unrelated viral infections

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a drug or small portfolio of drugs that safely produces meaningful clinical benefit against serious infections caused by several biologically distinct viral families. Its defining feature is useful treatment breadth across unrelated viruses, rather than activity against only one infection or closely related group. It does not require a single medicine that treats every virus. This is the proposed concept, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Conceptual synthesis: breadth could reside in an individual drug or emerge collectively from a complementary portfolio. Those are different accomplishments and should be reported separately: a portfolio covering several families does not establish that each component has cross-family activity. Laboratory suppression of multiple viruses would be an intermediate result; the intended innovation requires benefit in patients at tolerable doses.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment: a clinically effective portfolio spanning unrelated viral families could expand treatment options across several serious infections and reduce dependence on developing a separate medicine for each pathogen. The revolutionary feature would be the combination of breadth, safety and clinical usefulness. Broad laboratory activity alone would not deliver that change.

Such treatments could potentially be used before a precise diagnosis, but only where their demonstrated coverage includes the plausible causes of illness and prescribing criteria identify appropriate patients. Breadth would not eliminate the need for diagnosis: identifying the pathogen and assessing treatability could still determine whether a drug is suitable, which portfolio component to use and whether another treatment is needed.

A pre-existing portfolio could also provide an early treatment option during some new outbreaks. That possibility depends on the emerging virus being susceptible, an effective dosing regimen being established, acceptable safety in the affected population and sufficient availability. Activity against previously tested members of a family does not guarantee activity against every newly emerging member. Affordability, production and distribution are additional requirements; accessibility does not follow automatically from antiviral breadth.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed technical challenge: achieve a sufficiently shared vulnerability across unrelated viruses while preserving a useful margin between antiviral activity and harm to the patient. The research identifies viral diversity and dependence on host cells as central barriers: differences in replication machinery complicate shared targeting, while interference with cellular functions can introduce toxicity. These are coherent development challenges, but their scientific basis is not documented by the accessible content retained in the supplied evidence.

Conceptual synthesis: the breakthrough must bridge laboratory activity and clinical benefit. A candidate would need to work at exposures that patients can tolerate and under the conditions in which serious infections are actually treated. Its useful spectrum must also remain sufficiently dependable despite viral evolution. For a portfolio, complementary coverage must be established explicitly rather than inferred from a collection of promising individual results.

The remaining engineering and clinical task is therefore to establish which infections are treatable, at what doses, in which patients and with what resistance risks. Neither a shared biological target nor activity across a finite laboratory panel would by itself resolve those questions. The supplied material does not identify a demonstrated mechanism or candidate portfolio that has overcome these barriers.

current_state.text: The research states that existing antivirals have transformed treatment for several specific infections while effective therapies remain unavailable for many others. Those background claims remain unverified within this supplied evidence package. No assessable trial results, approved-drug inventory, quantitative efficacy findings or cross-family treatment demonstrations are included, so the package cannot establish the present extent of either antiviral success or the remaining treatment gap.

The supplied bibliographic record identifies a review attributed to Thibaut et al., titled “Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses,” with a stated publication date of 7 October 2026 and DOI 10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1. According to the supplied review, however, the retained HTML contains only a cookie-access message. The article identity, authors, publication date, abstract and substantive contents could not be verified from that artifact. The earlier description of access as a review abstract must therefore be corrected.

The source index records retrieval on 11 November 2026 and a saved extraction of 153 characters. Although its mechanical fields mark the artifact as verified and not truncated and list no extraction issues, the supplied review establishes that the retained text provides no identifiable article content. Successful saving of an access page does not establish access to the intended scientific document. The review also reports an empty bounded search record, so freshness of the treatment landscape cannot be assessed.

Consequently, the supplied material establishes neither a clinically validated cross-family portfolio nor a universal antiviral. This is a limit on the available evidence, not evidence that such results are false or that the concept is infeasible. Even if the listed review’s identity were confirmed, its stated focus on direct-acting agents against RNA viruses would require care when relating its conclusions to the broader concept of treatment across unrelated viral infections.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized clinical trials should show clinically meaningful benefit and acceptable safety for the same drug or a clearly defined small portfolio against serious infections from multiple biologically distinct viral families. Trial protocols should specify the patient populations, treatment timing, comparator, clinical outcomes and magnitude of benefit considered meaningful. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established consensus standards; the supplied material supports no particular numerical threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Meaningful clinical benefit and acceptable safety across distinct viral families

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth assessment: the evidence should identify every tested virus and family, explain their biological diversity and distinguish the spectrum of each drug from the combined spectrum of the portfolio. Reproducible findings across independent studies and relevant patient populations would strengthen confidence. A finite set of successful tests establishes demonstrated breadth within that set, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Reported tested-virus breadth distinguishes individual drugs from the portfolio

completion_criteria.text: Proposed prospective assessment: testing against newly emerging members should map susceptibility, effective dosing and resistance risks, including failures and uncertain results. Laboratory susceptibility could justify further investigation but would not automatically establish clinical effectiveness for a new outbreak. Follow-up should determine whether resistance or other changes materially narrow the usable spectrum.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective testing maps emerging-virus susceptibility, dosing and resistance risks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: a convincing demonstration should make clear where treatment is suitable and where evidence is absent, including safety restrictions and conditions for use before precise diagnosis. Claims of outbreak readiness should additionally establish availability and deployability. Claims of accessibility should be supported separately by evidence about cost, supply and delivery rather than inferred from pharmacological performance.
completion_criteria.label: Reported treatment boundaries identify suitable uses and evidence gaps

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: INF-05, near-patient diagnosis of the cause and treatability of most serious infections, is a direct complement. Better diagnosis could guide selection from an antiviral portfolio and identify infections outside its coverage. INF-07 could potentially support treatment while diagnostic results are pending, but its success would not complete the diagnostic objective.

INF-08, a pre-emptive vaccine against diverse pandemic coronaviruses, and INF-09, a rapid end-to-end vaccine response to a newly identified pathogen, share the outbreak-preparedness goal. Their central intervention is vaccination, whereas INF-07 concerns treatment of infection. Cross-family antiviral coverage is also a different breadth requirement from protection across diverse coronaviruses. INF-01, a broadly protective HIV vaccine, likewise pursues prevention rather than the treatment capability defined here.

INF-02, a safe scalable cure for established HIV infection, and INF-11, a treatment-free cure for chronic hepatitis B, overlap through antiviral treatment but demand distinct cure outcomes. A medicine could improve illness or suppress viral activity without producing a durable treatment-free cure. Conversely, a cure for one infection would not establish efficacy across unrelated viral families.

INF-10, prevention of multiple sclerosis by controlling Epstein–Barr virus, and INF-14, mechanism-guided prevention of major post-viral syndromes, concern consequences associated with viral infection. Effective acute antiviral treatment might become relevant to those objectives, but that is a conditional possibility requiring separate evidence. Benefit against an acute infection would not by itself establish prevention of multiple sclerosis or a post-viral syndrome.

INF-06, a dependable platform for generating new antibacterial treatments, and INF-15, a rapidly adaptable clinical phage-therapy platform, share drug-development and adaptable-treatment concerns but address bacterial infections. INF-03 and INF-12 address tuberculosis vaccination and curative treatment; INF-04 and INF-13 address malaria vector control and vaccination. Their prevention, transmission and treatment goals belong to the same infectious-disease portfolio, but success in INF-07 would not establish coverage of these nonviral infections or complete their separate objectives.

unresolved_issues: The listed review’s bibliographic identity, publication date, abstract and substantive contents remain unverified from the retained artifact.
The supplied evidence does not establish the current inventory of effective antivirals, the extent of unmet treatment needs or any demonstrated clinically effective cross-family portfolio.
The empty bounded search record prevents assessment of landscape freshness; the artifact’s retrieval date does not resolve that limitation.
The intended portfolio size, target infections and families, and allocation of breadth among individual drugs remain unspecified.
Clinically meaningful benefit thresholds, acceptable safety boundaries and the required biological diversity of demonstrations remain to be defined for particular indications.
Prospective susceptibility, resistance, prediagnostic prescribing and practical access requirements remain to be established.
The relationship between the listed review’s stated RNA-virus scope and the broader viral-treatment concept cannot be assessed without its scientific content.

brief.title: Medicines for unrelated viral infections
possible: People with serious viral infections could receive a medicine, or one of a small set, that works against several unrelated groups of viruses. Doctors could also have an early treatment option during some new outbreaks.
why: Patients would gain treatment options across several serious infections. A small set of medicines with complementary coverage could reduce the need to develop a separate treatment for each virus.

sources.showed: Their review describes medicines that act directly on viruses and the biological factors that determine which viruses they can treat.
sources.cited_for: It explains the case for a complementary set of medicines with broader coverage.
sources.not_established: A review does not demonstrate safe, effective treatment across unrelated viral groups.

sources.showed: Patients receiving remdesivir recovered faster from Covid-19 than those receiving a placebo, a treatment without the active drug.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates a patient benefit from an antiviral medicine.
sources.not_established: Benefit against Covid-19 does not establish benefit against unrelated viral infections.

sources.showed: Zotatifin suppressed viruses from five families, biologically distinct groups, in laboratory cells.
sources.quote: Zotatifin also effectively inhibited multiple arboviruses (Chikungunya, Una, and Zika viruses), influenza A virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, and vaccinia virus.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates that an individual compound can suppress unrelated viruses in cells.
sources.not_established: Cell experiments do not establish effective treatment at doses patients can tolerate.

sources.showed: In a preprint, the experimental compound cAIMP protected mice against chikungunya virus (CHIKV). Other cell experiments found that tested drugs differed in which viruses they inhibited.
sources.quote: In addition, cAIMP provided protection against CHIKV in a CHIKV-arthritis mouse model.
sources.cited_for: It supports animal testing and explicit mapping of each drug's coverage and failures.
sources.not_established: Protection in mice and activity in cells do not establish safe treatment across unrelated infections in patients.

shown: Beigel and colleagues demonstrated faster recovery with remdesivir in patients with Covid-19. Valdés-Torres and colleagues demonstrated broader activity with zotatifin in laboratory cells. These are separate steps toward combining patient benefit with coverage across unrelated viruses.
missing: Trials still need to demonstrate meaningful benefit and acceptable safety across unrelated infections for the same medicine or a defined small set.
Each medicine's coverage, effective doses and risk of viruses evolving to evade treatment need to be established.
Suitable patients, rules for treatment before diagnosis, and practical outbreak supply and delivery need to be established.

milestones.label: Safe patient benefit across unrelated viral groups
milestones.explanation: Trials with randomly assigned treatments would have to show meaningful benefit and acceptable safety across unrelated infections for the same drug or defined small set. This would establish useful treatment breadth.

milestones.label: Clear coverage for each medicine and the whole set
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to identify each virus and distinguish each drug's coverage from the combined coverage. This would establish how broadly each treatment works without implying it treats every virus.

milestones.label: Emerging viruses tested for treatment response
milestones.explanation: Testing as new viruses emerge would have to map whether treatment works, effective doses and risks of viruses evolving to evade it. This would reveal whether usable coverage holds up as viruses change.

milestones.label: Clear treatment boundaries and conditions for use
milestones.explanation: Results would have to define suitable uses, safety limits, gaps and rules for treatment before diagnosis. Outbreak readiness would also require availability and delivery; access claims would require evidence on cost and supply.

uncertain: The size of the medicine set, target infections and division of coverage among drugs remain undefined.
What counts as meaningful benefit, acceptable safety and sufficiently unrelated viral groups must be decided for particular uses.
Activity against known viruses may not predict treatment success against newly emerging relatives.

page.title: Cross-family antivirals for respiratory infections
page.definition: A single antiviral with a new mechanism of action against influenza has FDA approval to treat uncomplicated influenza and at least one respiratory infection caused by a virus from another family. A family is a taxonomic group. Influenza viruses and coronaviruses, for example, belong to different families.

goal.need: Seasonal influenza causes about a billion cases worldwide each year, including 3–5 million severe illnesses. Influenza and COVID-19 can cause the same symptoms, yet flu antivirals are not expected to help patients with COVID-19. One medicine could shorten illness when started early in outpatients with either of the infections it covers. In a new outbreak, an existing treatment could spare patients the wait for a drug to be developed from scratch if clinical testing showed benefit against the new virus.

statements.quote: seasonal and pandemic influenza A, influenza B, and at least one other respiratory virus
statements.context: Area 9.1 of Broad Agency Announcement BAA-23-100-SOL-00004, amendment 7, asks for evidence of antiviral efficacy across these viruses for an outpatient treatment.

completion.title: FDA approves one antiviral to treat uncomplicated influenza and a respiratory infection from another family.
completion.criterion: FDA-approved prescribing information for the same antiviral covers treatment of uncomplicated influenza and at least one respiratory infection caused by a virus from a different family. The drug has a new mechanism of action against influenza. BARDA’s clinical target is clinically meaningful earlier symptom relief versus untreated patients when treatment begins within 48 hours of symptom onset.
completion.set_by: BARDA Influenza & Emerging Infectious Diseases Division, respiratory broad-spectrum antiviral target product profile: Goal 1, multiple-family objective, and Indication for Use and Clinical Efficacy table rows; FDA determines marketing approval.
completion.threshold_quote: Indicated for treatment of influenza and at least one other respiratory virus
completion.basis: BARDA’s indication threshold specifies influenza plus one other respiratory virus. Its multiple-family objective supplies the cross-family scope. The symptom endpoint is a BARDA development target. FDA determines which treatment indications the evidence supports.

milestones.title: One candidate inhibits influenza and a respiratory virus from another family in cells.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate in cell culture that the same candidate inhibits an influenza virus and at least one respiratory virus from another family.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, integrated readiness component 3B for activity in vitro and respiratory antiviral target product profile for family coverage.

milestones.title: A candidate antiviral demonstrates animal efficacy and undergoes initial toxicity and exposure studies.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate animal efficacy at the intended dose, schedule, duration and route, with initial toxicity and pharmacokinetic studies (BARDA 4A–4B). A study published on 2 December 2021 found that oral 4′-fluorouridine reduced RSV lung virus in mice (5 mg/kg daily, started 24 hours after infection; n=5/group) and SARS-CoV-2 shedding in ferrets (20 mg/kg daily, started 12 hours after infection; n=3–4/group). These findings establish the efficacy component across two respiratory virus families.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels table, components 4A and 4B. The criteria are stated in the table.

milestones.title: A candidate antiviral completes Phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic assessment in people.
milestones.criterion: Once the investigational new drug application may proceed, complete a Phase 1 assessment of initial safety and pharmacokinetics, meaning how drug exposure changes over time in people. Assess immune responses where applicable.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, integrated readiness components 6B and 6C, and FDA’s investigational new drug process.
milestones.threshold_quote: an initial safety, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity assessment

milestones.title: A candidate antiviral completes Phase 2 trials assessing safety and efficacy in infected people.
milestones.criterion: Complete a controlled Phase 2 study in patients with an infection for which treatment is sought. Evaluate effectiveness for the studied indication and assess common short-term side effects and risks.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b), and BARDA, integrated readiness component 7B.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluate the effectiveness of the drug for a particular indication or indications

milestones.title: Pivotal trials establish an antiviral's clinical benefit for both respiratory indications.
milestones.criterion: Establish clinical benefit and characterise safety for the same antiviral in each claimed patient population, including uncomplicated influenza and a respiratory infection caused by a virus from another family. BARDA’s target is clinically meaningful earlier symptom relief compared with untreated patients when treatment begins within 48 hours of symptom onset.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Step 3: Clinical Research, Phase 3 treatment-benefit criterion; BARDA respiratory antiviral target product profile, Clinical Efficacy table row.
milestones.threshold_quote: Researchers design Phase 3 studies to demonstrate whether or not a product offers a treatment benefit to a specific population.

milestones.title: FDA submissions cover both respiratory treatment indications for the same antiviral.
milestones.criterion: Submit to FDA the evidence and proposed prescribing information for both uses of the same antiviral. The uses may be covered by original marketing applications or by a supplement seeking the remaining indication after the first is approved.
milestones.set_by: FDA, guidance on separate marketing applications and supplements, and BARDA, integrated readiness component 8B.
milestones.threshold_quote: If the initial application is approved, the application can be subsequently supplemented to add a new indication.

milestones.title: One candidate outperforms oseltamivir in an influenza model and shows efficacy in a second family.
milestones.criterion: Show superior efficacy to oseltamivir in a therapeutic influenza animal model. Show efficacy of the same candidate in an animal model for at least one other respiratory virus of pandemic potential from a different family.
milestones.set_by: BARDA, respiratory broad-spectrum antiviral target product profile, Nonclinical Efficacy threshold and multiple-family objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: Must demonstrate superior efficacy to oseltamivir in therapeutic influenza animal models

milestones.title: Animal studies assess initial toxicity, drug exposure and drug effects.
milestones.criterion: Complete initial animal toxicity studies and determine pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in appropriate animal models, with immune response assessed as applicable. BARDA accepts studies outside formal Good Laboratory Practice at this stage.
milestones.threshold_quote: initial non-GLP toxicity studies and determine pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics

not_found: No numerical minimum for clinically meaningful symptom shortening was found in BARDA's respiratory antiviral target product profile.
No FDA approval or marketing application covering the specified influenza and other-family respiratory indications was located.

results.finding: cAIMP reduced CHIKV-associated footpad swelling and viral load in 5–6 mice.
results.detail: The animal result concerns CHIKV, not a respiratory infection. The text does not report initial pharmacokinetic studies or establish toxicity assessment at the intended clinical regimen.
results.quote: cAIMP drug treatment at 6 or 12 hours post-CHIKV infection provides long-term therapeutic benefit by reducing footpad swelling CHIKV viral load (n=5–6 mice).

results.finding: In influenza-infected ferrets (n=3), oral 4’-fluorouridine at 2 mg/kg reduced viral shedding.
results.detail: The study reports animal efficacy and initial mouse pharmacokinetic measurements, but does not report an initial animal toxicity study or establish that the tested regimen is the intended treatment regimen.
results.quote: Once-daily oral treatment of ferrets with 2 mg/kg 4’-FlU initiated 12 hours after infection rapidly stopped virus shedding and prevented transmission to untreated sentinels.

results.finding: In a Phase 2b/3 nitazoxanide trial enrolling 624 people, median symptom duration was 95.5 hours in the 600 mg group with confirmed influenza.
results.detail: The placebo median was 116.7 hours (p=0.0084). The trial assessed adverse events but ended with about 60% of the planned number of influenza-infected participants because the influenza season ended. The efficacy result concerns influenza alone.
results.quote:
The 
median duration of symptoms for participants receiving placebo was 116·7 h (95% CI 108·1–122·1) compared with 
95·5 h (84·0–108·0; p=0·0084) for those receiving 600 mg nitazoxanide and 109·1 h (96·1–129·5, p=0·52) for those 
receiving 300 mg nitazoxanide.

results.finding: Oral MDL-001 reduced SARS-CoV-2 lung titers by 2.9 log10 in mice (n=9/group).
results.detail: Oral 250 mg/kg BID, first dose 1 h before infection; also oral PK and no treatment-related adverse findings across 376 animals in 17 studies.
results.quote: Oral MDL-001 reduced lung viral titers at Day 3 p.i. by 2.9 log 10  versus vehicle ( Supplementary Table S3 ).

results.finding: Remdesivir shortened median recovery by 5 days versus placebo among 1,062 randomized adults hospitalized with COVID-19.
results.detail: Median time from symptom onset to randomization was 9 days. Recovery meant discharge or remaining hospitalized without a medical need for ongoing care.
results.quote: Patients in the remdesivir group had a shorter time to recovery than patients in the placebo group (median, 10 days, as compared with 15 days; rate ratio for recovery, 1.29; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.12 to 1.49; P<0.001)

results.finding: Zotatifin significantly lowered infectious titers of influenza A, vesicular stomatitis virus, and vaccinia virus at 24 hours in two independent A549 experiments run in triplicate.
results.detail: The paper cites earlier coronavirus studies for zotatifin’s activity against respiratory viruses from another family.
results.quote: Zotatifin treatment led to a statistically significant reduction in viral titers for all three viruses

results.finding: Remdesivir inhibited 3 non-influenza respiratory viruses in human cell cultures (n=2 independent experiments).
results.detail: The source reports qualitative inhibition for these respiratory viruses without a numerical effect size in the text.
results.quote: Interestingly, the direct-acting antiviral drug remdesivir, a nucleoside analogue, was not effective against CHIKV and WNV, but exhibited potent antiviral effects against SARS-CoV-2, RSV (respiratory syncytial virus), and EV-D68.

results.finding: cAIMP induced antiviral gene expression in mouse footpad tissue at 24 hours (n=5 mice per group).
results.detail: The efficacy study monitored body weight. The source reports no dedicated animal toxicity study or measurements of drug exposure over time.
results.quote: Graph shows the transcriptional activation of STING/type 1 IFN genes in the left footpad at 24 h after drug treatment (n=5 mice/group).

results.finding: 4’-FlU inhibited pandemic H1N1 in differentiated human airway epithelial culture at an EC90 of 0.07 μM (n = 3 per concentration).
results.quote: 4’-FlU inhibited a panel of relevant influenza A and B viruses with nanomolar to sub-micromolar potency in HAE cells.

results.finding: 4’-FlU yielded 100% survival in a therapeutic mouse model of lethal pandemic H1N1 (group size unspecified in the supplied text).
results.detail: The study’s H5N1 animal results concern another influenza A subtype in the same virus family.
results.quote: Three doses mediated complete survival when treatment was initiated up to 60 hours after infection, indicating a broad time window for effective intervention.

results.finding: 4’-FlU reached a peak plasma concentration of approximately 1 μM in mice after a single oral dose (sample size unspecified in the supplied text).
results.detail: The cited cytotoxicity measurement comes from cultured human airway epithelial cells.
results.quote:
Free 4’-FlU reached a maximal plasma exposure of approximately 1 μM 90 minutes after oral administration, far exceeding the cell culture EC
90
concentration against the influenza virus test panel.

results.finding: In 300 infected adults, 18% of molnupiravir recipients reported an adverse event.
results.detail: Follow-up continued through day 14. No adverse event required withdrawal of molnupiravir.
results.quote:
Частота пациентов с зарегистрированными 
случаями НЯ составила 23,67% (71/300): в группе 
препарата молнупиравир — 18,00% (27/150), в 
группе плацебо — 29,33% (44/150).

results.finding: In 300 adults with influenza and/or another acute respiratory viral infection, molnupiravir shortened mean clinical recovery by 0.82 days versus placebo.
results.detail: The analysis pooled 149 influenza-only, 143 other respiratory viral infection, and 8 mixed-infection cases. The pooled estimate cannot establish clinically meaningful earlier relief in each indication.
results.quote:
Разница 
средних значений времени (в днях) до наступления 
клинического выздоровления между группой 
препарата молнупиравир и плацебо составила 
-0,82 дня, 95% ДИ для разницы средних составил 
[-1,20; -0,43] дня.

results.finding: In at-risk COVID-19 outpatients (n=1,408 analyzed), molnupiravir lowered the risk of hospitalization or death by 3.0 percentage points versus placebo.
results.detail: The prespecified interim analysis was the formal efficacy test. The 3.0-percentage-point estimate comes from the final modified intention-to-treat analysis.
results.quote:
6.8% (48 of 709 participants) in the molnupiravir 
group as compared with 9.7% (68 of 699 par -
ticipants) in the placebo group (difference, 3.0 
percentage points; 95% CI, −5.9 to −0.1).

results.finding: MDL-001 inhibited influenza and other respiratory viruses across 13 cell-culture test entries, with EC90 values of 47–595 nM.
results.detail: The sample size counts respiratory virus test entries. The text describes technical replicates but gives no replicate count.
results.quote: MDL-001 inhibited influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, SARS-CoV-2 and variants of concern, endemic human coronaviruses, and hepatitis B, C, and D viruses with nanomolar potency.

results.finding: MDL-001 reduced H1N1 lung viral RNA by 2.6 log10 in mice (n = 3 per group), meeting the study’s equivalence margin versus oseltamivir.
results.detail: Influenza dosing began 24 hours before infection. SARS-CoV-2 dosing also began before infection.
results.quote: MDL-001 demonstrated equivalent in vivo efficacy to oseltamivir against mouse-lethal influenza A virus infection, reducing lung viral load by 2.6 log 10  and preventing weight loss and mortality.

results.finding: MDL-001 produced zero treatment-related adverse findings with oral dosing across a preclinical dataset of 376 rodents.
results.detail: Initial safety monitoring covered clinical signs, body weight and mortality across efficacy, pharmacokinetic and dedicated safety studies.
results.quote: MDL-001 was well tolerated across 376 individual animals, with no treatment-related adverse findings by oral administration at dosing up to twice daily for 28 days ( Supplementary Table S11 ).

results.finding: Molnupiravir Phase 1 in 130 healthy volunteers reported zero serious adverse events.
results.detail: One participant stopped dosing because of a rash and completed all scheduled assessments. Dose escalation stopped after plasma exposure exceeded the level projected to be efficacious from animal models.
results.quote: No subjects experienced serious adverse events.

results.finding: Tizoxanide inhibited all 13 day-5 influenza isolates from nitazoxanide-treated participants.
results.quote:
Viruses present in all 13 samples were 
inhibited by tizoxanide, with eﬀ  ective concentrations 
EC50 and EC90 similar to those inhibiting viruses present 
in the corresponding baseline samples (data not shown).

results.finding: Among 16 participants in the nitazoxanide PK substudy, mean tizoxanide AUC over 12 h in the higher-dose arm was 29.1 µg·h/mL.
results.detail: The analysis included six participants at 300 mg and ten at 600 mg.
results.quote:
Mean area under the curve (AUC 0–12 h ) for tizoxanide 
plasma concentrations were 12·6 μg × h/mL (SD 9·2) for 
the nitazoxanide 300 mg group and 29·1 μg × h/mL 
(33·8) for the nitazoxanide 600 mg group.

results.finding: Among 257 patients with confirmed influenza, high-dose nitazoxanide shortened median time to symptom relief by 21.2 h versus placebo.
results.detail: Recruitment ended with about 60% of the planned influenza-positive sample. The lower dose did not significantly shorten time to symptom relief.
results.quote:
The 
median duration of symptoms for participants receiving placebo was 116·7 h (95% CI 108·1–122·1) compared with 
95·5 h (84·0–108·0; p=0·0084) for those receiving 600 mg nitazoxanide and 109·1 h (96·1–129·5, p=0·52) for those 
receiving 300 mg nitazoxanide.

results.finding: Among 257 patients with confirmed uncomplicated influenza, high-dose nitazoxanide shortened median time to symptom relief by 21.2 h versus placebo.
results.detail: Too few participants had any individual non-influenza viral infection for meaningful analysis. The symptom-relief result in participants without a documented virus could not establish benefit for a second viral indication.
results.quote:
The 
median duration of symptoms for participants receiving placebo was 116·7 h (95% CI 108·1–122·1) compared with 
95·5 h (84·0–108·0; p=0·0084) for those receiving 600 mg nitazoxanide and 109·1 h (96·1–129·5, p=0·52) for those 
receiving 300 mg nitazoxanide.

results.finding: NHC inhibited RSV plaque formation in 1 of 2 reported assay types. Sample size was unreported.
results.detail: The authors identify the underlying assay data as data on file.
results.quote:
Additional in vitro evaluation 
of NHC against RSV found that the compound 
inhibited plaque formation but was inactive 
in a cytopathic effect assay [data on file].

results.finding: Molnupiravir versus placebo in 45 adults with experimental RSV infection and evaluable primary endpoint data yielded p = 0.201 for viral-load AUC.
results.detail: The symptom-resolution finding was secondary and the analyses used no multiplicity adjustment.

results.finding: EIDD-2801 improved H1N1 mouse survival over oseltamivir by 12.5 percentage points (12 mice assigned per group).
results.detail: The paper gives the initial group size but does not clearly reconcile it with the survival percentages after scheduled tissue collection. It reports no significance test for the survival difference. Four hamsters per group were sampled for tissue analysis.
results.quote:
Unexpectedly, EIDD-2801 treatment exhibited higher protection efficacy (62.5%) than oseltamivir phosphate (50%) in H1N1-UI182-infected mice (Fig.
1
C), highlighting its superior antiviral potential.

results.finding: Favipiravir alone reduced mean lung SARS-CoV-2 titer to 22.4% of vehicle control in Syrian hamsters (n = 4 per group).
results.detail: The lung titer reduction after the lower challenge dose was not statistically significant. Favipiravir did not improve body weight changes under the tested conditions.
results.quote: Therapeutic administration of favipiravir (dosages on days 1 to 3: 300 mg/kg, twice/day) also reduced virus titers in the lungs after a high-dose challenge (mean titer reduced to 22.4% of the control group)

results.finding: Enisamium in adults with mixed respiratory infections (n=100) increased day-14 full recovery by 60.8 percentage points versus placebo.
results.detail: The recovery difference uses the Results counts (56/60 vs 13/40). The abstract gives 93.9% for enisamium, while the Results report 93.3%, consistent with 56/60. Investigators were unblinded.
results.quote: At day 14, 93.3% ( n  = 56) of the FAV00A-treated patients had fully recovered, whereas only 32.5% ( n  = 13) of patients in the placebo group returned to normal health status.

results.finding: In hospitalized adults with oxygen-requiring COVID-19 (n=285), enisamium shortened median time to clinical improvement by 1 day versus placebo.
results.detail: Median time from symptom onset to randomization was 8 days. In the subgroup randomized less than 5 days after onset (n=33), median time to clinical improvement was 8 days with enisamium and 13 days with placebo.
results.quote: Overall, patients in the enisamium group reached the primary endpoint after a median of 10 days compared to a median of 11 days for patients in the placebo group

results.finding: In adults with mild COVID-19 (n=232 analyzed), Ingavirin shortened mean time to clinical recovery by 47.8 hours versus placebo.
results.detail: Clinical recovery required all 16 COVID-19 symptom scores to be mild or absent. The recovery hazard ratio was 1.462 (95% CI 1.123–1.904).
results.quote:
Patients in 
the experimental group demonstrated faster clinical recovery (by 47.8 h) and alleviation of intoxication and individual catarrhal 
symptoms.

results.finding: VV251 inhibited influenza A and RSV in cell culture (n = 3 independent experiments), with an influenza A EC₅₀ of 0.2052 μM.
results.quote: In this study, preliminary  in vitro  studies indicated that VV251 exhibits potent inhibitory efficacy against both RSV and IAV, with EC 50  values ranging from nanomolar to low micromolar.

results.finding: Molnupiravir Phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic assessment was completed in 32 healthy adults, with zero adverse-event discontinuations.
results.detail: This repeat-dose trial extended earlier short-duration assessments. The paper reports regulatory approval to conduct the trial without identifying the specific IND record.
results.quote: No serious AEs, deaths, or discontinuations due to AEs were reported.

results.finding: In a completed Phase 2a COVID-19 trial (202 dosed), molnupiravir shortened median SARS-CoV-2 RNA clearance by 1 day versus placebo.
results.detail: The trial measured symptom duration and found no statistically significant difference. It lacked statistical power to evaluate clinical endpoints such as symptom duration or hospitalization.
results.quote: The primary endpoint of this phase 2a study was the median time to viral clearance, and the difference between participants who received 800 mg of molnupiravir compared with placebo was 1 day.

results.finding: Single-dose studies of molnupiravir or NHC in mice, rats, and dogs reported 0 deaths (animal counts unstated).
results.detail: The EMA considered the pivotal toxicity species appropriate based on their pharmacokinetic profiles. The exploratory studies identified tolerability effects despite the absence of mortality.
results.quote:
Single dose toxicities studies were incorporated into preliminary non-GLP exploratory studies in mice, rats 
and dogs with a top dose utilised in each study of 2000 mg/kg. No mortality was seen in any of the studies.

definition = "A single antiviral with a new mechanism of action against influenza has FDA approval to treat uncomplicated influenza and at least one respiratory infection caused by a virus from another family. A family is a taxonomic group. Influenza viruses and coronaviruses, for example, belong to different families.". Reason: The definition omits the US approval authority, the uncomplicated influenza indication and the new influenza mechanism that distinguish the stated goal.

goal.need = "Seasonal influenza causes about a billion cases worldwide each year, including 3\u20135 million severe illnesses. Influenza and COVID-19 can cause the same symptoms, yet flu antivirals are not expected to help patients with COVID-19. One medicine could shorten illness when started early in outpatients with either of the infections it covers. In a new outbreak, an existing treatment could spare patients the wait for a drug to be developed from scratch if clinical testing showed benefit against the new virus.". Reason: The current rationale gives an agency objective but omits what cross-family coverage would change for patients and when that benefit could extend to an outbreak.

add statement by Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA), 2026: "seasonal and pandemic influenza A, influenza B, and at least one other respiratory virus". Reason: The two existing statements concern pandemic preparedness broadly, while BARDA explicitly names the respiratory viruses one candidate must cover.

edit completion: title = "FDA approves one antiviral to treat uncomplicated influenza and a respiratory infection from another family."; criterion = "FDA-approved prescribing information for the same antiviral covers treatment of uncomplicated influenza and at least one respiratory infection caused by a virus from a different family. The drug has a new mechanism of action against influenza. BARDA\u2019s clinical target is clinically meaningful earlier symptom relief versus untreated patients when treatment begins within 48 hours of symptom onset."; threshold_quote = "Indicated for treatment of influenza and at least one other respiratory virus"; threshold_ref = 3; basis = "BARDA\u2019s indication threshold specifies influenza plus one other respiratory virus. Its multiple-family objective supplies the cross-family scope. The symptom endpoint is a BARDA development target. FDA determines which treatment indications the evidence supports."; refs = [3, 6]. Reason: The current title describes approval for a virus, and the criterion omits the uncomplicated influenza population named in the product profile.

edit m1: title = "One candidate inhibits influenza and a respiratory virus from another family in cells."; criterion = "Demonstrate in cell culture that the same candidate inhibits an influenza virus and at least one respiratory virus from another family."; set_by = "BARDA, integrated readiness component 3B for activity in vitro and respiratory antiviral target product profile for family coverage."; threshold_quote = "in vitro activity of candidate(s)"; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 3]. Reason: The cell test currently counts unrelated virus families even without influenza and embeds one candidate’s results in the criterion.

split m2 into "One candidate outperforms oseltamivir in an influenza model and shows efficacy in a second family." | "Animal studies assess initial toxicity, drug exposure and drug effects.". Reason: Animal efficacy and initial toxicity are separate BARDA tests, and the efficacy criterion omits the influenza comparator and the evidence required for a second respiratory virus.

edit m3: criterion = "Once the investigational new drug application may proceed, complete a Phase 1 assessment of initial safety and pharmacokinetics, meaning how drug exposure changes over time in people. Reason: The Phase 1 criterion embeds preliminary poster results and lacks the quoted threshold for a completed human assessment.

edit m4: criterion = "Complete a controlled Phase 2 study in patients with an infection for which treatment is sought.
